what is the user trying to accomplish?
is the practice of describing user intentions and goals at multiple levels of specificity — from a broad analytic purpose down to the precise data manipulations that purpose requires.
A chart, dashboard, or infographic built around clearly stated questions is easier to design, build, and evaluate than one built by intuition.
The heart of task abstraction is the idea that user behavior can be conceptualized as a hierarchy of actions that go from abstract ideation and intent to concrete activity with a specific tool.
It describes in formal terms how we move from ideas to artifacts.
One conceptualization of this hierarchy comes from Gotz and Zhou (2008).
They de visual analytic activity in four tiers, from most abstract to most concrete.
A high-level analytic goal, stated in domain terms
A specific analytical question that contributes to the task
A concrete analytic move — a data or visualization operation
A single software interaction that carries out the action
A task-level question describes what a user wants to accomplish in the data.
Independent of any specific chart or interaction.
Do not name a chart type, a widget, or a gesture.
A public-health researcher should recognize it as a real question without knowing what a scatter plot is.
Open-ended enough to allow more than one design.
If only one chart obviously answers it, the question is probably a sub-task in disguise.

. This means avoid vague terms like “relate” or “most” and instead consider translating these into concepts like correlation or relative frequency. The language here will depend on the familiarity of the domain expert with statistical and scientific methods.
“Can the user select a country from a dropdown to see a bar chart of spending over time?”

This question names a widget (dropdown) and a chart type (bar chart).
It skips past the analytic goal and lands directly on a design decision.
“How has healthcare spending changed across countries over the past two decades?”

This describes the analytic goal without committing to any design.
It could be answered with a line chart, a heat map, a choropleth, or a small-multiples display.

A well-known vocabulary for action verbs is from Amar et al. These are called “analytic primitives”.
What is the exact value of this item?
What is an aggregate — a sum, average, or ratio?
What is the maximum or minimum?
In what order do these items rank?
What are the minimum and maximum values overall?
What is the overall shape of these values?
Which items are most similar to one another?
These are based on observed user interactions with data visualization tools.
Gotz and Zhou propose something more granular, based on grouping actions by intent.

Because of the variety of vocabulary types, we distinguish between
actions and leave room for other intentions, domains, and levels of action.

The Target names the data feature the action is applied to.
Common targets:
Patterns of change over time or across a dimension
The spread and shape of a set of values
The maximum or minimum of a set
Relationships between two or more variables
How does healthcare spending relate to life expectancy?
Which countries achieve high life expectancy despite low spending?
Which countries spend less than $1,500 per capita on healthcare?
Does the relationship plateau above a certain threshold?
What is the average life expectancy at each spending level?

The two operations use different Amar primitives.
Filter selects a subset of items; Compute Derived Value produces an aggregate across groups.
Finally, events are the hardware and software levers we pull to produce concrete results.

## The Full Picture

Here is a complete hierarchy for one example.

Subtasks are coded as $S_n$ and actions as $A_n$.

| Level | Question | Form |
|-------|----------|------|
| **Task** | How does healthcare spending relate to life expectancy? | Plain domain question |
| $S_1$ | Which countries achieve high life expectancy despite low spending? | Specific analytical question |
|     $A_1$ | Which countries spend less than $1,500 per capita? | Filter + Spending |
| $S_2$ | Does the relationship plateau above a certain spending threshold? | Specific analytical question |
|     $A_2$ | What is the average life expectancy at each spending level? | Compute Derived Value + Life Expectancy |

Each level is more specific than the one above it.

The two sub-tasks approach the task from different angles.

The two operations use different Amar primitives.
